title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations
authors: Harikrishnan Vijayakumaran, Shunyu Yin, Martin Abendroth, Miguel A. Bessa, Karl A. Kalina
abstract: Neural network material models can represent yield surfaces and hardening laws with far more flexibility than classical closed-form plasticity formulations, but training such a model end-to-end through an implicit return map introduces non-trivial challenges. This work presents a thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive model for rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity that jointly learns a flexible yield function together with its evolution laws. For non-associative flow, the yield function extends the convex flow potential by a jointly trained additive term, which renders the model thermodynamically consistent by construction. Isotropy and convexity are enforced simultaneously across all learnable components through a permutation-invariant, spectral (eigenvalue-based) representation. Training proceeds through a backward-Euler return map, with gradients propagated by the implicit function theorem together with an eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware scheme for safe differentiation. The robustness and generality of the approach are demonstrated by reproducing known constitutive models, including non-associative flow, learning material behavior from stress--strain data extracted from a full-field finite element simulation, and capturing unknown non-associative behavior from homogenized representative volume elements of a foam. Finally, the proposed neural plasticity model is evaluated within finite element simulations to solve boundary-value-problem under plane stress.

infographic.key_insight: A spectral neural constitutive model learns flexible yield surfaces and evolution laws while enforcing isotropy, convexity, and thermodynamic consistency by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables learned elastoplastic material laws, including non-associative flow, to be used in finite element boundary-value simulations.
method: Use permutation-invariant eigenvalue representations to enforce isotropy and convexity across learnable components.
Represent non-associative yielding through a jointly learned additive extension of a convex flow potential.
Train through a backward-Euler return map using implicit-function gradients and eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware differentiation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation includes reproducing known constitutive models, learning from full-field finite element stress–strain data and homogenized foam responses, and solving plane-stress boundary-value problems.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires careful differentiation near repeated eigenvalues and robust implicit return-map solves; the stated scope is rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations

title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
authors: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart
abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

infographic.key_insight: Recurrent neural operators can approximate microstructure-dependent homogenized viscoelastic laws, with a sufficient internal-variable dimension growing logarithmically in inverse relative stress error and material contrast.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These surrogates aim to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations while generalizing across loading histories and heterogeneous material properties.
method: Use internal variables to approximate loading-history dependence with Markovian dynamics.
Represent microstructure-dependent constitutive responses with neural operators.
Use a spectral memory-kernel representation to prove uniform approximation for periodic Kelvin–Voigt materials in 2D and 3D.
infographic.evidence_signal: Viscoelasticity and crystal-plasticity experiments examine internal-variable dimension and sample complexity, while the theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation guarantees concern periodic Kelvin–Voigt viscoelasticity; comparable guarantees for nonlinear crystal plasticity are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity

title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium
authors: Marius Nevland, Kundan Kumar, Inga Berre, Jakub Wiktor Both, Eirik Keilegavlen
abstract: This paper studies the numerical approximation of a mathematical model of coupled flow and viscoelastic deformation in a fractured porous medium including fracture contact mechanics. We consider a mixed-dimensional model, where the fracture is modeled as a co-dimension one object within the porous medium. This model couples Darcy flow in the matrix and fracture, linear viscoelasticity of the matrix and frictional contact mechanics of the fracture surfaces; the contact conditions include normal compliance and a Coulomb friction law. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution is established, and stability and a priori error estimates are derived. A numerical experiment is performed in which numerical error estimates are computed and compared to the theoretical results.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete mixed-dimensional model couples porous flow, viscoelastic deformation and frictional fracture contact, with proven discrete well-posedness, stability and a priori error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliable simulation of fractured porous materials where fluid flow, deformation and frictional contact interact.
method: Represent fractures as co-dimension-one interfaces with Darcy flow in both matrix and fractures.
Couple linear viscoelasticity to normal-compliance contact and Coulomb friction.
Discretize using conforming finite elements in space and implicit Euler time stepping.
infographic.evidence_signal: A numerical experiment computes errors and compares them with the theoretical estimates.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports a numerical error study, not experimental validation or demonstrated large-scale performance.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium

title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs
authors: Guangyu Wang, Xiaodong Ma, Xinming Wu
abstract: Natural fractures (NFs) and drilling-induced tensile fractures (DITFs) in acoustic image logs provide insights into rock mass structure and in situ stress, but manual characterization is time-consuming. Deep learning can automate this task, although expert-labeled data are scarce. We investigate whether adapting a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM) outperforms task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations. Using 80 annotated acoustic image samples, we fine-tuned DINOv3, pretrained on satellite imagery, and evaluated it on four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning. The adapted model estimated NF and DITF parameters comparably to human interpretation. Relative to U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch, it yielded fewer false positives and negatives and more accurate fracture counts and orientations. However, its performance advantage generally narrowed as training sample size decreased. We also assessed decoder architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and image enhancement. A progressive upsampling decoder with full fine-tuning performed best among the DINOv3 configurations tested, while fracture-focused image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of VFM adaptation for fracture characterization in acoustic image logs with limited labeled data and suggest a transferable workflow for other annotation-scarce geoscientific imaging tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting pretrained DINOv3 improved fracture characterization in acoustic image logs over task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated characterization of natural and drilling-induced tensile fractures can support rock mass assessment and in situ stress interpretation.
method: Fine-tune satellite-imagery-pretrained DINOv3 on annotated acoustic image logs.
Compare against U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch.
Test decoders, fine-tuning strategies, and fracture-focused image enhancement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 80 annotated samples and four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning, the adapted model estimated fracture parameters comparably to human interpretation and produced fewer detection errors than the baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The performance advantage generally narrowed with fewer training samples; image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs

title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
authors: Yeyuan Liu
abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent advantages of real neural wiring can reflect physiology tuning rather than connectivity, and some conclusions reverse under independently constrained physiology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational model comparisons, match optimisation effort and independently constrain constitutive parameters before attributing performance gains to structural fidelity.
method: Compare real-wiring physiology transferred to nulls (P1) with separate tuning for each wiring (P2).
Restrict separate tuning to physiology consistent with independent data (P3).
Test robustness using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the mushroom-body model, real wiring beat a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but lost by 0.09 under P3; 95% confidence intervals excluded zero, and held-out runs confirmed the reversal.
infographic.watch_item: Failure at imaging-consistent physiology indicates model inadequacy, not necessarily a defect in biological wiring; some other structural claims remained robust.
infographic.paper_title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology

title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for higher-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs
authors: Gourab Panigrahi, Phani Motamarri
abstract: The time to solution of an iterative solver depends on the number of iterations and the cost per iteration. This paper develops algorithms that reduce both for elliptic problems discretized with high-order continuous finite elements on distributed GPUs, implemented in a unified matrix-free code supporting CUDA, HIP and SYCL. A distributed direct fast-diagonalization (FD) Poisson solver provides exact solutions on tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction. Its tensor data stay distributed, moved between slab layouts by collective transposes or kept in place by a Schur-complement approach. It is also an exact coarse solver. A two-level hybrid Schwarz preconditioner with FD cell solves (HS-FD) is extended to 2:1 hanging-node octrees with exact local cell inverses, while a \(p\)-multigrid preconditioner with Chebyshev--Jacobi smoothing (CJ-\(p\)MG) resolves hanging-node constraints at every level within fused kernels. Both approaches exploit FP32, where cell shapes and coefficients allow, within an FP64 conjugate-gradient iteration, adaptively select replicated or distributed coarse levels, support block solves for multiple right-hand sides and determine all parameters from the operator without case-specific tuning. Comparisons with Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients (Jacobi PCG), MFEM, nekRS and deal.II span uniform, graded and octree meshes, layered coefficients, and four applications across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs. The direct solver is two to three orders of magnitude faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes. HS-FD converges in 11 iterations for an octree generalized Poisson problem across 8 to 1024 MI250X graphics compute dies. The results guide solver selection by mesh structure and coefficients

infographic.key_insight: Matrix-free fast diagonalization and tailored preconditioners accelerate high-order finite element elliptic solves on distributed GPUs by reducing both iteration counts and per-iteration cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster elliptic solves can reduce computational bottlenecks in large-scale engineering simulations using high-order finite elements.
method: Distributed exact fast-diagonalization solver for supported tensor-product meshes and coefficient structures.
Hybrid Schwarz with exact FD cell inverses and p-multigrid with fused hanging-node constraint handling.
FP32 acceleration within FP64 conjugate gradients, adaptive coarse-level distribution, and CUDA/HIP/SYCL support.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests span uniform, graded and octree meshes across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs: direct FD is 100–1,000× faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes, while HS-FD converges in 11 iterations across 8–1,024 MI250X graphics compute dies for an octree generalized Poisson problem.
infographic.watch_item: Exact direct FD requires supported tensor-product structure and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction; FP32 acceleration also depends on cell shapes and coefficients.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for higher-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs

title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
authors: Suhas Chandrashekar, Thomas Stieglitz, Prasanth Velvaluri
abstract: Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

infographic.key_insight: Finite element simulations indicate that thermally stressed NiTi-based bilayer hinges can drive prescribed origami folding while reducing unit-cell dimensions by approximately 50% relative to previously reported designs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact, self-folding structures could support minimally invasive delivery and controlled deployment of neurovascular implants.
method: Model thermal-mismatch bending in thin-film NiTi–molybdenum and NiTi–SS316L composites.
Optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape using finite element simulations.
Integrate hinges into a waterbomb origami unit cell to assess coordinated folding.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation-based hinge optimization and coordinated folding in a complete waterbomb unit cell, but no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Microscale fabrication tolerances and safe thermal actuation in vivo remain implementation concerns not validated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework

title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
authors: Henrique Oliveira
abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).

infographic.key_insight: F3-AGI v4.0 combines gated learning, residual program synthesis, and active exploration to improve sample-efficient abstract reasoning on CPUs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its compute-saving learning and search mechanisms may inform resource-constrained engineering AI, but the abstract reports no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Mistake-gated plasticity with Fisher-EMA preconditioning and virtual ATP gating.
Complexity-guided program synthesis with residual patches and smallest-pair early rejection.
512D random projections for Expected Free Energy exploration and dead-signature pruning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Offline CPU evaluation with zero LLM calls solved 57/400 ARC-AGI-1 tasks (14.25% pass@2) at 1.62 s/task mean latency, including 38/350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The modest hold-out solve rate and synthetic or local auxiliary benchmarks limit claims of broad generalization.
infographic.paper_title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning

title: Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt
authors: Duy-Cuong Bui, Trung-Anh Dang, Vincent Nguyen, Duc V. Le, Ngoc-Son Vu
abstract: Prompt-based continual learning adapts a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by tuning a small set of prompt tokens. Recently, one-prompt methods which share one single prompt across all tasks make this paradigm maximally parameter efficient. The open question is how a shared prompt can keep the knowledge of old classes while being updated for new ones. Existing methods protect old knowledge in parameter space, where they freeze task-specific prompts, expand new components, or sparsely gate which tokens receive gradients. However, this method sacrifices plasticity, yet the drift it still permits in shared tokens can corrupt the prompt's function on past classes. What must be preserved is the prompt's behavior. We propose TEA-Prompt, which couples (i) a token evaluation module that assigns each prompt token a continuous, input-conditional relevance score injected into the attention logits, softly specializing tokens across tasks without discarding any of them, and (ii) an attention-behavior anchoring loss that constrains each token's attention output around class-specific query regions using only compact Gaussian query statistics without stored old images, weighted by the token's past relevance. Anchoring the attention value allows the parameters to continue updating freely, as long as their interaction remains unchanged. TEA-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters. Code is publicy available at https://github.com/cuonga1cvp/TEA-Prompt.git

infographic.key_insight: TEA-Prompt preserves a shared prompt’s attention behavior rather than freezing its parameters, enabling adaptation to new classes while reducing forgetting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach may support memory-efficient continual adaptation of engineering vision systems, but the abstract does not demonstrate solid mechanics or constitutive modeling applications.
method: Adapt a frozen vision transformer using one shared prompt.
Softly specialize prompt tokens with input-dependent relevance scores injected into attention logits.
Anchor attention outputs using compact class-specific Gaussian query statistics, weighted by past token relevance, without storing old images.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art accuracy and markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify accuracy gains or test whether Gaussian query statistics remain adequate under engineering-domain shifts.
infographic.paper_title: Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt

title: Multiscale LegONet: Learning Coefficient-Dependent Local Spaces for Composable Multiscale Finite Elements with Localized Error Bounds
authors: Yueqi Wang, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Guang Lin
abstract: We introduce multiscale LegONet (Ms-LegONet), a plug-and-play learned block for heterogeneous elliptic problems. One network per spatial dimension is trained once on local coefficient patches and reused, without retraining, across coefficient layouts, sources, boundary data and domain sizes within the trained coefficient class. On a fixed primitive patch the network maps the local coefficient to a zero-boundary space, the only learned object. The multiscale basis functions are the harmonic extensions of a fixed set of boundary traces, each a Galerkin solve in that space. Shared interface traces enforce continuity, larger blocks are assembled by recursive static condensation without any parent-scale network, and a localized Céa bound attributes the error of the learned spaces primitive by primitive. The training labels are harmonic responses of single patches, so no global solve enters the training. Against MsFEM, GMsFEM, the neural-operator element method and an end-to-end Fourier neural operator, Ms-LegONet is the most accurate at equal unknowns: its $L^2$ error is $4$ to $150$ times below the baselines on two-dimensional mosaics of $256$ high-contrast primitives, and its median error stays within $0.1$ percentage points of that of exact local spaces in three-dimensional layered media. For each new coefficient it is $1.6$ to $2.3$ times faster than a fine-grid direct solve in two dimensions. In three dimensions it computes the many-query port response of a chain $30$ to $900$ times faster than finite element solves on the same or a finer mesh, at a relative error of $10^{-4}$ against their $6\%$ and $1.6\%$.

infographic.key_insight: Ms-LegONet learns reusable, coefficient-dependent local finite-element spaces that compose into larger solvers with localized error bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It accelerates heterogeneous elliptic simulations while allowing changes in coefficient layouts, loads, boundary data and domain size without retraining within the trained coefficient class.
method: Train one network per spatial dimension on local coefficient patches and patch-level harmonic responses, without global training solves.
Predict zero-boundary spaces, then compute multiscale basis functions through local Galerkin harmonic extensions with shared interface traces.
Assemble larger blocks by recursive static condensation and attribute approximation error to individual primitives using a localized Céa bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 4–150× lower L² errors than baselines at equal unknowns on 2D mosaics, 1.6–2.3× speedups over fine-grid direct solves in 2D, and 30–900× speedups for 3D many-query port responses.
infographic.watch_item: Reuse is restricted to the trained coefficient class; accuracy for out-of-distribution material patterns requires separate validation.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale LegONet: Learning Coefficient-Dependent Local Spaces for Composable Multiscale Finite Elements with Localized Error Bounds

title: Are UFOs Real? Introducing Unified Factored Organizers
authors: Thomas X. Sheppard, Alon Albalak, Joel Lehman, Kenneth O. Stanley
abstract: Implicit in much research in deep learning is the assumption that if a network achieves low loss, then it must have learned a good representation of its training data. Recent work by Kumar et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.11581) questions this assumption, arguing that networks trained with conventional gradient descent achieve low loss despite learning fractured entangled representations (FER), leaving related concepts disconnected and unrelated concepts entangled inappropriately. Kumar et al. further show that dramatically better representations are possible: a network evolved through an open-ended, human-in-the-loop process learned unified factored representations (UFR) that capture the regularities of the domain far better than a counterpart with nearly identical outputs trained with conventional gradient descent. Inspired by UFR, this paper introduces unified factored organizers (UFOs), networks trained to model regularities in the representations of other networks. A network can then be trained both to achieve low loss on its task objective and to align its representations with the model learned by the UFO. Networks trained with UFOs are shown to learn qualitatively superior representations in an image-regression domain where representations are easily interpretable. To provide quantitative evidence for the impact of UFOs on representation learning, a transformer is trained with and without UFO regularization to grok a modular arithmetic problem set. When combined with weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 10x relative to weight decay alone. Without weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 100x relative to an unregularized baseline. If UFOs are real, they suggest a new paradigm where loss functions themselves are trained to learn an effective model of good representation.

infographic.key_insight: Unified factored organizers (UFOs) learn regularities in another network’s representations and guide training toward better-organized internal features, not just low task loss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: UFO regularization could inform representation learning for computational mechanics surrogates, but this paper does not evaluate fracture, damage, or other mechanics applications.
method: Train a UFO network to model regularities in a target network’s representations.
Train the target network using both task loss and alignment with the UFO’s learned model.
Evaluate representation quality in image regression and grokking speed in modular-arithmetic transformers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports qualitatively better image-regression representations and over 10× fewer transformer training steps to grok with UFOs plus weight decay versus weight decay alone, and over 100× fewer without weight decay versus an unregularized baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from interpretable image regression and modular arithmetic; transfer to engineering datasets and total computational overhead remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Are UFOs Real? Introducing Unified Factored Organizers

title: PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots
authors: Shaohong Zhong, Marco Pontin, Perla Maiolino
abstract: Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives. However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently. A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation. Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation. Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines. Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks.

infographic.key_insight: PneuGen uses collaborating LLM agents and simulation feedback to efficiently co-design soft pneumatic robots for specified tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps engineers explore coupled geometry, morphology, material, and actuation choices for task-specific soft robots.
method: A designer agent proposes design programs using a parametric component library.
Fitted module response models supply physical priors linking geometry and pressure to deformation.
Automated validation and finite-element simulation generate diagnostics that a critic agent uses to recommend revisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports significant gains over computational optimisation baselines on grasping and planar/3D shape matching, ablation support for both the critic and response models, and real-world demonstrations.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested tasks remains uncertain, and broader use may require additional component models and simulation validation.
infographic.paper_title: PneuGen: Task-Driven Agentic Co-Design of Soft Pneumatic Robots

title: A transversely isotropic constitutive model for semisoft elasticity in main-chain liquid crystal elastomers
authors: Donghao Li, Xin Yi, Fan Feng
abstract: Monodomain main-chain liquid crystal elastomers exhibit pronounced stiffness anisotropy and broad semisoft plateaus following finite onset strains. At fixed chain anisotropy, the neo-classical model predicts equal principal Young's moduli, while its transversely isotropic extension with a constant semisoft modulus constrains the relation between reorientation onset and subsequent stress growth. We develop a finite-strain, isothermal elastic model combining transversely isotropic network elasticity with a deformation-dependent quadratic semisoft penalty. Within a weak-fluctuation approximation, a reduced statistical closure based on assumed linear contraction of effective local anisotropy fluctuations at fixed mean anisotropy yields an exponential transition from an initial to a residual semisoft modulus. The network energy preserves ideal soft modes, and the formulation recovers the de Gennes strain-director coupling in the infinitesimal limit. Analytical relations for perpendicular tension show that the rotating-stage stress depends on both the current semisoft modulus and its derivative with respect to the first deformation invariant. This permits a finite onset followed by a substantially flatter rotating response than in the constant-modulus limit. Oblique tension couples director rotation, shear and lateral contraction. Comparisons with orientation-dependent measurements using a common parameter set capture the principal stiffness contrast and broad perpendicular plateau, with discrepancies remaining in oblique stresses and intermediate-angle initial moduli.

infographic.key_insight: A transversely isotropic model with a deformation-dependent semisoft modulus captures stiffness anisotropy and allows finite reorientation onset followed by a broad, flatter stress plateau.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports mechanical analysis of main-chain liquid crystal elastomers whose stiffness and deformation response depend strongly on loading direction.
method: Combine finite-strain, isothermal network elasticity with a deformation-dependent quadratic semisoft penalty.
Use a weak-fluctuation statistical closure to obtain an exponential transition from initial to residual semisoft modulus.
Derive perpendicular-tension relations and couple director rotation, shear and lateral contraction under oblique tension.
infographic.evidence_signal: Comparisons with orientation-dependent measurements using one common parameter set capture the principal stiffness contrast and broad perpendicular plateau.
infographic.watch_item: Discrepancies remain in oblique stresses and intermediate-angle initial moduli, limiting confidence for off-axis predictions.
infographic.paper_title: A transversely isotropic constitutive model for semisoft elasticity in main-chain liquid crystal elastomers

title: An open source Python code for three-dimensional topology optimization in single precision on a consumer GPU
authors: Leonilson Toffoli Pedrini, Rodolfo G. M. Andrade, Rafael M. Ferro
abstract: Three-dimensional topology optimization solves linear systems with millions of unknowns at every design iteration. Consumer graphics cards run far faster in single than in double precision, and open codes for them mostly address minimum compliance. This educational article presents TOF3D, an open source Python code for density-based topology optimization in single precision on one consumer GPU. It solves four classes of problems: stress constrained minimum compliance, robust minimum compliance against manufacturing errors, compliant mechanisms and bone-like porous infill. The stiffness operator is applied without assembly, and the conjugate gradient method is preconditioned by geometric multigrid. Rounding the element matrix to single precision gave rigid body motions a spurious energy and changed compliances by up to 5.4%. Forming the element products from differences of nodal displacements reduced this error to $1.3\times 10^{-5}$ at no cost in time. Adjoint sensitivities agreed with finite differences to within $1.7\times 10^{-6}$, and the solutions agreed with Ansys Mechanical APDL to within $4.1\times 10^{-10}$ with the same element. On an RTX 3060 with 12 GB, one design iteration of a cantilever took 0.46 s with 0.5 million elements and 15 s with 33.5 million. On the same card and problem, an open GPU code that applies its operator in double precision took 3.7 and 21 s with 0.5 and 4.2 million elements and ran out of memory on larger meshes. Eight cases fixed in a protocol before the runs took 9 to 35 minutes each with 4.2 to 5.2 million elements.

infographic.key_insight: TOF3D enables large-scale 3D topology optimization on a single consumer GPU by using displacement differences to avoid accuracy loss in single-precision stiffness calculations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source Python code makes stress-constrained, manufacturing-robust, compliant-mechanism and porous-infill design accessible on a 12 GB GPU.
method: Density-based topology optimization with matrix-free stiffness application.
Conjugate gradient solver preconditioned by geometric multigrid.
Element products formed from nodal displacement differences to suppress spurious rigid-body energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported compliance error fell from up to 5.4% to 1.3×10⁻⁵; on an RTX 3060, cantilever iterations took 0.46 s for 0.5 million elements and 15 s for 33.5 million.
infographic.watch_item: Single precision requires careful operator implementation: directly rounding element stiffness matrices introduced spurious rigid-body energy.
infographic.paper_title: An open source Python code for three-dimensional topology optimization in single precision on a consumer GPU

title: Convergence of an adaptive multilevel stochastic Galerkin FEM driven by a residual-based error estimator
authors: Alex Bespalov, Maximilian Brunner, Alexander Freiszlinger, Dirk Praetorius
abstract: In this paper we analyze a residual-based a posteriori error estimation strategy and adaptive multilevel algorithms for a class of parametric elliptic PDEs, where the diffusion coefficient depends on countably many uncertainty parameters. Under a saturation assumption on the parametric approximation space, we propose a computable residual-based error estimator. We also introduce the notion of K-compatibility of finite element meshes, which ensures that only the triangulations with comparable mesh sizes are used, and incorporate this concept into the adaptive algorithm. We prove that the estimator is reliable and satisfies K-dependent stability and reduction properties. These results underpin our convergence analysis of the adaptive multilevel algorithm: we show that the algorithm drives both the a posteriori error estimator and the true approximation error to zero. Numerical experiments illustrate and confirm the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A residual-driven adaptive multilevel stochastic Galerkin FEM provably reduces both its error estimator and true approximation error to zero under the stated assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports reliable finite element simulation of elliptic problems with uncertain material coefficients represented by countably many parameters.
method: Construct a computable residual-based error estimator under a parametric saturation assumption.
Enforce K-compatibility so coupled finite element meshes have comparable mesh sizes.
Establish estimator reliability, K-dependent stability and reduction, and adaptive convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence proofs and numerical experiments that illustrate and confirm the theoretical findings.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on parametric saturation, while enforcing K-compatible meshes introduces a constraint on adaptive refinement.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence of an adaptive multilevel stochastic Galerkin FEM driven by a residual-based error estimator

title: Heterogeneous and episodic permeability evolution and correlation with acoustic emission activity during faulting in granite
authors: Ado Farsi, Franciscus M. Aben, Nicolas Brantut
abstract: Rock permeability changes dramatically during brittle deformation, affecting faulting dynamics and crustal fluid flow. Here, we combine fluid-flow and local pore-pressure measurements acquired during a quasi-static shear-failure test in Westerly granite with a three-dimensional finite-element inverse method. The measured flow rate and six internal pore pressures constrain the local hydraulic transmissivities (permeability-thickness products) of ten cells along the growing fault. Synthetic ensembles anchored to the pressure-sensor accuracy recover these transmissivities with median mean errors of 7-9%, with the fault ends generally better resolved than the interior. Applied to the experiment, the method resolves episodic transmissivity increases, interspersed with decreases, through fault growth and slip. Local values reach approximately $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ m$^3$ (16 times the bulk contribution), and the final-stage values vary by a factor of 2.3 along the fault. Across cells, the median absolute change in recovered transmissivity is at most about 16% for $\pm50\%$ changes in assumed fault-zone thickness. The local one-dimensional estimates of Aben et al. (2024) agree in scale with the three-dimensional results, with a median 3-D/apparent ratio of 0.81. Cumulative acoustic-emission counts track the overall hydraulic evolution, but the relations of local event density, its stagewise increments and amplitude-weighted activity to transmissivity vary between cells. The comparison distinguishes the value of AE for mapping damage growth from quantitative hydraulic prediction using event-count and relative-amplitude metrics.

infographic.key_insight: Fault transmissivity in granite evolves unevenly and episodically, while acoustic-emission activity tracks overall damage but does not consistently predict local hydraulic changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spatially resolved hydraulic estimates can improve assessments of fault-controlled fluid flow where uniform permeability or acoustic-emission proxies may miss local variations.
method: Conduct a quasi-static shear-failure test in Westerly granite with fluid-flow and six internal pore-pressure measurements.
Invert measurements using a 3-D finite-element model to recover transmissivity in ten cells along the growing fault.
Compare recovered transmissivities with acoustic-emission counts, spatial density and amplitude-weighted activity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic ensembles yielded median mean recovery errors of 7–9%; experimental local transmissivities reached approximately 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ m³ and varied by a factor of 2.3 along the final-stage fault.
infographic.watch_item: Interior fault cells were less well resolved than the ends, and results from this laboratory test require validation before field-scale application.
infographic.paper_title: Heterogeneous and episodic permeability evolution and correlation with acoustic emission activity during faulting in granite

title: A new approach to measuring both the steady flow curve and the planar extensional viscosity of complex fluids using exponential shear
authors: Nicholas King, Eugene Pashkovski, Reid Patterson, Gareth H. McKinley
abstract: We revisit the protocol known as Exponential Shear (ES), first proposed by Doshi and Dealy in 1986. This is a transient strong flow that can be readily imposed in the laboratory using commercial strain-controlled (separate motor and transducer) rheometers which accurately measure both the (exponentially) time-varying torque and normal force exerted by the sample. Numerous studies over the years have proposed competing definitions of an appropriate material function for reporting data obtained from the exponentially time-varying imposed deformation. We revisit this unresolved challenge and carefully reconsider the exponential material kinematics involved and the proper definition of the corresponding material functions. We show that by understanding the time-varying eigenvalues and eigenvectors of both the shearing kinematics and the evolving state of stress in the sample it is, in fact, possible to use an exponential shear test to quantitatively map out \textit{both} the full flow curve (of shear viscosity vs. shear rate) and the steady planar extensional viscosity curve as a function of deformation rate. These findings are supported by numerical simulations of a number of nonlinear viscoelastic constitutive models, asymptotic analysis, as well as experiments with several polymeric liquids.

infographic.key_insight: Exponential shear testing can recover both the steady shear flow curve and the steady planar extensional viscosity curve by accounting for evolving deformation and stress directions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables broader characterization of complex-fluid rheology using commercial strain-controlled rheometers that measure time-varying torque and normal force.
method: Impose an exponentially increasing shear deformation.
Analyze the evolving eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the flow kinematics and sample stress.
Define material functions that map measurements to shear and planar extensional viscosity curves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports support from nonlinear viscoelastic constitutive-model simulations, asymptotic analysis, and experiments with several polymeric liquids.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable implementation requires accurate transient torque and normal-force measurements; applicability beyond the tested polymeric liquids remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A new approach to measuring both the steady flow curve and the planar extensional viscosity of complex fluids using exponential shear

title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
authors: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song
abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.

infographic.key_insight: A parameterized physics-informed neural network predicts embedded microfluidic cooling performance across a continuous geometric design space with reported computational savings exceeding four orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast thermohydraulic predictions could accelerate the design and optimization of embedded manifold microchannels for high-performance chip cooling.
method: Use four geometric dimensions and three spatial coordinates as network inputs.
Combine geometric ansatz embedding, SOAP optimization, and a thermal-conductivity-based learning curriculum.
Train with an optimized JAX backend on a single consumer-grade GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against finite-element simulations, the abstract reports relative errors of 8.1% for velocity and 5.6% for temperature, with training convergence in under four hours.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish experimental validation or accuracy outside the evaluated geometric and operating ranges.
infographic.paper_title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling

title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
authors: Calum S. Skene, Jeffrey S. Oishi, Keaton J. Burns, Moritz Linkmann, Geoffrey M. Vasil, Alexander Morozov
abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.

infographic.key_insight: The simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) model predicts a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both channel and pipe flows, highlighting the importance of transient rheology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These predictions could help engineers assess viscoelastic flow stability under realistic conditions and discriminate between constitutive models.
method: Numerically analyse linear stability of pressure-driven sPTT channel and pipe flows without inertia.
Explore instability across polymer concentrations and Weissenberg numbers.
Contrast sPTT predictions with models sharing its steady rheology and laminar profiles.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical results identify instability across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers than previously predicted for purely elastic channel instability.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical linear instability, not experimental validation or proof of subsequent chaotic flow.
infographic.paper_title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid

title: A Functional Preservation Score for Auditing Connectome Operations: Compression, Alignment, Transport, and Local-Rule Writing
authors: Praveg Vashishtha
abstract: We introduce the Functional Preservation Score (FPS), a null-normalised, behaviourally grounded measure of how much of a neural network's input-output function survives a structural operation, and use it to audit the operations underlying speculative "mind-migration" pipelines on public data that runs on a single laptop. Across five pre-registered studies on the C. elegans connectome, whole-brain calcium activity, and hippocampal replay, FPS yields two positive characterisations and a three-part negative. Low-bit quantisation of a real connectome exhibits a structure-dependent sparsity floor: uniform int4/ternary quantisation is forced to roughly 73%/98% effective sparsity because heavy-tailed integer synaptic weights round to zero, while mixed-precision protection of hub neurons lowers these floors to about 27%/32%. Decoded hippocampal replay sequences compress heavily yet remain identifiable at a cross-validated top-1 accuracy of 0.69 (95% CI [0.63, 0.74]; chance 0.125; permutation p < 1e-3) from latents of order 10-50 bits per event, and a bounded incremental store shows a graceful-versus-cliff capacity trade-off. The migration pipeline fails in simulation at each stage for largely independent reasons: the putative "identity payload" is not a functionally separable module (p >= 0.16 at every tested size); cross-individual functional transport via Gromov-Wasserstein collapses once the target's wiring is respected (fidelity 1.00 to 0.40, [0.31, 0.49], p < 1e-3) or alignment is imperfect (0.06, [0.00, 0.13]); and biologically plausible local plasticity cannot reach the function the target topology provably admits (gap 0.45, [0.27, 0.64], p < 1e-3, d = 2.0). We release FPS, the data loaders, and all operations as a toolkit. All results are at nematode / small-network scale and concern coherence in simulation, not the feasibility of reading or writing a living brain.

infographic.key_insight: Functional Preservation Score (FPS) audits whether network operations preserve input–output behavior, revealing useful compression but independent failures in simulated identity separation, cross-network transport, and local-rule writing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: FPS offers a behavior-based audit for neural-network compression and transfer, showing that structural compatibility alone does not ensure functional preservation.
method: Measure functional preservation using a null-normalised, behaviorally grounded score.
Audit quantisation, module separation, Gromov–Wasserstein alignment and transport, and local plasticity.
Evaluate replay compression and bounded incremental storage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Five pre-registered studies used public connectome, calcium-activity, and hippocampal-replay data; replay identification reached 0.69 cross-validated accuracy versus 0.125 chance, while wiring-constrained transport fidelity fell from 1.00 to 0.40.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern nematode-scale and small-network simulations, not the feasibility of reading, writing, or migrating a living brain.
infographic.paper_title: A Functional Preservation Score for Auditing Connectome Operations: Compression, Alignment, Transport, and Local-Rule Writing
